name: Sree Poornathrayeesa Temple — Vrischikolsavam
tagline: Thrippunithura’s eight‑day Vrischikam festival of elephants, processions and Panchari melam
summary: Vrischikolsavam is the eight‑day annual ulsavam of Sree Poornathrayeesa Temple in Thrippunithura (Vrischikam, Nov–Dec), famous for twin daily processions, Panchari melam and nightly Kathakali.
description: Sree Poornathrayeesa’s Vrischikolsavam (Vrischikam, Malayalam month falling in November–December) is the temple’s main eight‑day ulsavam. The festival combines processional pageantry, high‑energy percussion (Panchari melam and thayambaka), nightly Kathakali and other classical/cultural programmes.

The festival matters because Poornathrayeesa is the historic royal deity of the old Cochin kingdom and the ulsavam marks one of Kerala’s earliest and most musically rigorous temple seasons — Tripunithura’s Panchari tradition is particularly prized by connoisseurs.

A visitor sees daily seeveli (morning) and vilakku ezhunnallippu (evening) processions with caparisoned elephants and full Panchari melams, cultural programmes after sunset (including Kathakali) and the concluding pallivetta and aarattu rituals on the final days.
Practical note: local listings publish the festival dates each year; check with the temple office or official Cochin Devaswom Board notices before you travel.
highlights: Eight‑day Vrischikam ulsavam (Nov–Dec) held at Sree Poornathrayeesa Temple
Seeveli (morning) and Vilakku Ezhunnallippu (evening) processions daily
Panchari melam — Tripunithura’s signature percussion tradition
Multiple caparisoned elephants accompany key processions
Nightly Kathakali and other classical/cultural performances

sections.heading: Background
body: Poornathrayeesa is worshipped here in a long royal tradition: the temple served as the family deity (rajadevata) of the erstwhile Cochin rulers and Vrischikolsavam evolved as a major rajotsavam over time.

The festival opens the Vrischikam season in Kerala and is known both for its ritual precision and its high standards of percussion performance. Many of the festival’s forms (Panchari, thayambaka, Kathakali) draw audiences from across Kochi and beyond.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend the two processions each day: morning seeveli and the evening vilakku ezhunnallippu. Both are accompanied by Panchari melam and caparisoned elephants; the tempo and tonal balance in Tripunithura’s Panchari are a highlight for percussion lovers.

Watch the nightly cultural schedule — Kathakali is regularly staged during Vrischikolsavam, and you will also find concerts, Ottanthullal and traditional solo/dance performances. The festival’s concluding days feature Pallivetta (ritual hunt) and aarattu (ceremonial bath of the deity).

Walk the streets around Kottakkakam Road and the temple precincts to experience local food stalls, artisans and the feel of the town during ulsavam nights; be prepared for crowds on the principal procession evenings.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Festival dates move each year with the Malayalam calendar. Local festival listings show Vrischikolsavam for 7–14 December 2026 (check the temple office/Devaswom Board before you travel). Expect early‑morning seeveli (around 7:30 am on normal days) and late‑evening vilakku ezhunnallippu (timings vary across festival nights).

Thrippunithura is on the Kochi Metro line and the temple is a short walk from the town centre; arrive early for the evening melams to find space and avoid congestion. Confirm parking and any local restrictions in advance during festival nights.

visitorInfo.bestTime: Vrischikam (Malayalam month; November–December) — festival nights for evening melam and processions.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Thrippunithura is served by Kochi Metro and local buses; the temple sits in town (Kottakkakam Road) and is a short walk from Thrippunithura centre. From Cochin International Airport expect a road journey of roughly 30–35 km (confirm transit time).
etiquette: Confirm the exact festival dates and programme with the temple office or Cochin Devaswom Board before you travel.
Use the Kochi Metro to Thrippunithura on busy evenings and arrive early for the main melams; streets get very crowded after sunset.
Dress modestly and follow temple rules; respect cordoned areas during processions and any instructions from temple volunteers.
Expect loud percussion and large crowds; secure equipment and keep children close during elephant processions.
